lead: Networked ECUs run software that can brake, steer or deploy an airbag, so a software fault can hurt people. Two standards deal with this. MISRA C is a set of coding guidelines that removes the risky parts of the C language, so embedded code behaves predictably and can be checked by tools. ISO 26262 is the functional-safety standard for road vehicles: it starts from a hazard, assigns an ASIL (automotive safety integrity level) from severity, exposure and controllability, and then demands documented evidence through a safety lifecycle. MISRA keeps the code clean; ISO 26262 shows the whole item is safe enough. Only a few universities teach this in depth.
prereq: You need the idea of determinism and fault confinement from CAN and CAN FD, and some C programming.

blocks.text: MISRA C:2012 sorts its guidelines as mandatory (never broken), required (broken only with a formal deviation) and advisory. A deviation is a written, reviewed permit with a reason and a risk analysis, not a silent exception. Typical rules: no recursion (stack depth must be provable); no use of malloc, calloc, realloc or free at all (Rule 21.3); no implicit conversion that can lose a value; braces round every if, else and loop body; pointer arithmetic only inside an array; every switch has a default; check every error return. A static-analysis tool checks the source, and the team fixes each violation or records a deviation.
Passing MISRA gives disciplined code; it is not proof of functional safety. Code generated from models must pass the same checks, or the generator must be qualified as a tool.

sections.h3: ISO 26262: hazard, ASIL, safety goal and evidence

blocks.text: ISO 26262:2018 has 12 parts and follows a V-model: requirements down the left side, implementation at the bottom, and verification and validation back up the right. Part 3 is the concept phase and part 6 covers software. The item definition fixes what is inside: which ECUs, sensors, actuators and functions. HARA (hazard analysis and risk assessment) studies each hazardous event and rates severity S0 to S3, exposure E0 to E4 and controllability C0 to C3. The standard's table gives the ASIL; for the classes S1 to S3, E1 to E4 and C1 to C3, it matches a simple sum: S + E + C = 10 gives ASIL D, 9 gives C, 8 gives B, 7 gives A, and 6 or less gives QM (quality management, no ASIL requirement).

Each hazardous event gets a safety goal that inherits its ASIL, such as "no unintended full braking at speed". The technical safety concept names safety mechanisms: plausibility checks, watchdog timers, redundant sensors, end-to-end protection of bus messages and a safe state. ASIL decomposition may split a requirement into two independent ones of lower ASIL, each still tagged with the original, for example ASIL B(D) + ASIL B(D), but the independence must be shown.

The fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) is the minimum time from a fault to a possible hazardous event. The safety mechanism must detect the fault and reach the safe state within it. Hardware is judged by architectural metrics computed from failure rates and the diagnostic coverage of the safety mechanisms: the single-point fault metric SPFM = 1 − (λSPF + λRF) ÷ λ, where λSPF is the rate of single-point faults, λRF the rate of residual faults and λ the total failure rate of the safety-related hardware, and the latent fault metric (LFM) for hidden faults. ASIL D asks for SPFM of at least 99 per cent.

examples.question: A brake-by-wire safety goal has FTTI = 200 ms. Sensor sampling takes 20 ms, a two-frame confirmation takes 40 ms and the actuator needs 30 ms to reach the safe state. How much time is left for the detection logic, and by when must the fault be flagged?
steps: Budget: detection time = FTTI − sampling − confirmation − actuation.
The fault must be flagged by 20 + 40 + 110 = 170 ms after it occurs.
The actuator then has 200 − 170 = 30 ms, so the safe state is reached at 200 ms, just inside the FTTI.
examples.answer: The detection logic has 110 ms; the fault must be flagged within 170 ms, and the actuator uses the last 30 ms.

examples.question: HARA rates unintended steering at motorway speed as S3 (life-threatening), E4 (high exposure) and C3 (hard to control), and a second hazard as S1 (light injuries), E4 and C2. Find the ASILs.
steps: Steering: S + E + C = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10, so ASIL D, the highest level.
If the steering controllability were C2 instead, the sum would be 9 and the ASIL C.
examples.answer: Unintended steering is ASIL D; the second hazard is ASIL A.

traps: MISRA compliance alone does not give ISO 26262 compliance: MISRA is coding evidence, while ISO 26262 also needs HARA, safety goals, a safety concept, metrics and verification.
ASIL D is the highest level, A the lowest; QM is not "ASIL 0" but means ordinary quality management with no ASIL requirement.
FTTI is not the detection time: it must hold sensing, confirmation, detection and actuation together.
ASIL decomposition does not lower the safety goal: each part keeps the original tag, such as B(D), and independence must be proved.
MISRA C:2012 bans the heap functions of stdlib.h outright (Rule 21.3); "no allocation after start-up" is a deviation some projects write, not the rule.

quiz.a: A documented, reviewed permit to break a required guideline, with a justification and a risk analysis.

quiz.q: Why does MISRA C ban recursion?
quiz.a: The depth of recursion, and so the stack use, is hard to bound, so the worst-case memory use cannot be proved.

quiz.q: FTTI is 150 ms; sampling 10 ms, confirmation 20 ms, actuator 20 ms. Find the detection budget.
A hazard is rated S2, E3, C3. Find the ASIL.
A team's code passes MISRA but it has done no HARA. Can it claim ASIL B?
quiz.a: No. Without HARA there is no safety goal or ASIL to meet. ASIL B also needs a safety concept, verification and confirmation measures; MISRA is only part of the software evidence.

quiz.q: An ASIL D requirement is decomposed. Give two allowed splits and what must be shown.
quiz.a: ASIL B(D) + ASIL B(D), or ASIL C(D) + ASIL A(D). The two parts must be sufficiently independent, with no common-cause failure, and together meet the ASIL D requirement.

beyond: Not for the exam. ISO 21448 (SOTIF) covers hazards from the limits of sensors and algorithms with no fault at all, and ISO/SAE 21434 covers cybersecurity. Industry keeps a traceable safety case in requirements tools and runs MISRA checkers in every build. Search for SOTIF, ISO/SAE 21434 and MISRA C:2023.
